questions.question: What two ingredients are needed for a semigroup?
options: A set, an identity element, and inverses.
A matrix and its determinant.
A set and an associative binary operation on it.
A vector space and an inner product.
questions.explanation: A semigroup is a set together with an associative binary operation on it.

questions.question: Does a semigroup have to contain an identity element?
options: No. An identity is not required for a semigroup.
Yes, and every element must also be invertible.
No, because semigroups are not allowed to have binary operations.
Yes. Every semigroup is automatically a monoid.

questions.source_support: Definition: semigroup requires an associative binary operation; monoid adds an identity.

questions.question: Why are products such as $a\star b\star c$ unambiguous in a semigroup?
options: Every element is its own inverse.
The operation is associative.
The set has exactly three elements.
The operation is necessarily commutative.
questions.explanation: Because the operation is associative, $(a\star b)\star c=a\star(b\star c)$, so products like $a\star b\star c$ are unambiguous regardless of grouping.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: repeated products such as $a\star b\star c$ are unambiguous.

questions.skill_detail: Interpret the role of associativity in semigroups.
option_explanations: Elements need not be their own inverses; a semigroup does not even require inverses (that is a group property), so inverses are irrelevant to the unambiguity of products.
The set can have any number of elements; $(\mathbb N,+)$ is a semigroup with infinitely many elements, and associativity — not set size — makes products unambiguous.
Commutativity is not required; associativity (not commutativity) is what removes grouping ambiguity, e.g. matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative.

questions.explanation: A group is a set with an associative binary operation (plus identity and inverses); since a semigroup only requires an associative operation, every group is a semigroup.

questions.question: On $\mathbb R$, is $a\star b=\max(a,b)$ a semigroup operation?
options: Only if the operation is not commutative.
No, because maximum is not closed on $\mathbb R$.
No, because maximum has no inverse for every element.
Yes, maximum is closed and associative.
questions.explanation: Yes — $\max$ is closed on $\mathbb R$ ($\max(a,b)\in\mathbb R$) and associative ($\max(a,\max(b,c))=\max(a,b,c)=\max(\max(a,b),c)$), so it is a semigroup operation.
questions.source_support: Definition: semigroup requires a closed associative binary operation.

option_explanations: Commutativity is not the issue; semigroups need not be commutative, and $\max$ is commutative anyway — what matters is closure and associativity.
$\max$ is closed on $\mathbb R$; the maximum of two real numbers is again a real number, so this objection is false.
Inverses are not required for a semigroup; only closure and associativity are needed, and $\max$ has both even though it has no inverses.

questions.question: On a set $A$, define $a\star b=a$. Does this make $A$ a semigroup?
options: Yes, the operation is associative.
No, because the operation is not closed.
No, because the operation ignores $b$.
No, unless $A$ has an identity element.
questions.explanation: Yes — $a\star b=a$ is closed (output in $A$) and associative ($(a\star b)\star c=a=a\star(b\star c)$), so $(A,\star)$ is a semigroup.
questions.source_support: Definition: semigroup requires an associative binary operation.

questions.skill_detail: Check associativity for a projection operation.
option_explanations: The operation is closed; its output is $a\in A$, so $a\star b\in A$ for all $a,b\in A$.
Ignoring $b$ does not break associativity; both $(a\star b)\star c$ and $a\star(b\star c)$ equal $a$, so the operation is associative.
An identity is not required for a semigroup; only closure and associativity are needed, and this operation has both without any identity element.

questions.question: Why are all $2\times3$ matrices not a semigroup under ordinary matrix multiplication?

questions.explanation: The product of two $2\times3$ matrices is not defined (shapes mismatch), so there is no binary operation and no semigroup.

questions.skill_detail: Check whether the operation is a binary operation before testing associativity.
option_explanations: The product is not merely non-associative; it is undefined.

A semigroup places no size limit on its underlying set, e.g. $(\mathbb R,+)$ is an uncountable semigroup, so cardinality is not the obstacle; the product of two $2\times3$ matrices is undefined because the inner dimensions $3$ and $2$ do not match, leaving no binary operation at all.
$2\times3$ matrices are not invertible (they are not square).
